title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
summary: India, Pakistan and China began their development paths around the same time with similar levels of income, yet followed different strategies and reached different outcomes. This chapter compares their strategies, demographic indicators, growth, sectoral structure and human development.

notes.heading: Why compare, and the common starting point
notes.html:
• All three are developing countries of Asia that started planned development at about the same time: India and Pakistan became independent in 1947 and the People's Republic of China was established in 1949.
  • Five-year plans began in India in 1951, in China in 1953 and in Pakistan in 1956.
  • Until the 1980s all three had similar growth rates and low per capita incomes.
  • Comparison helps a country understand its own strengths and weaknesses and learn from its neighbours in a globalised world where they are also competitors.

notes.heading: Development strategy of China
notes.html:
• State control: after 1949 all critical sectors, enterprises and land were brought under government control.
  • Great Leap Forward (1958): a campaign to industrialise on a massive scale; people were encouraged to set up industries in their backyards. In rural areas the commune system was introduced, under which people cultivated land collectively.
  • The campaign ran into problems: a severe drought caused famine deaths, and the withdrawal of Soviet professionals after a conflict with Russia hurt industrial projects.
  • Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (1966–76): launched by Mao; students and professionals were sent to work and learn in the countryside.
  • Reforms from 1978, introduced in phases: first in agriculture, foreign trade and investment; commune lands were divided into small plots allotted to households for use (not ownership), who kept the income after paying taxes. Later, private firms and township and village enterprises were allowed to produce goods.
  • Dual pricing: farmers and industrial units sold a fixed quantity at government prices and the rest at market prices.
  • Special Economic Zones (SEZs) were set up to attract foreign investors.

notes.heading: Development strategy of Pakistan
notes.html:
• Mixed economy with public and private sectors co-existing.
  • 1950s–60s: regulated policy framework for import-substituting industrialisation, combining tariff protection for consumer goods with direct import controls.
  • Green Revolution: mechanisation and public investment in infrastructure raised foodgrain output.
  • 1970s: nationalisation of capital goods industries.
  • Late 1970s and 1980s: shift towards denationalisation and encouragement of the private sector. Pakistan also received financial support from western nations and growing remittances from emigrants to the Middle East, which stimulated growth.
  • 1988: economic reforms were initiated.

India (recap)

Mixed economy with planning from 1951, emphasis on the public sector and import substitution, followed by the liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation reforms of 1991.

  • China's low growth is the result of the one-child norm introduced in the late 1970s. It also led to a decline in the sex ratio and will mean more elderly people relative to the young; China later relaxed the norm.

notes.heading: Growth, sectors and human development
notes.html:
GDP growth

China achieved very high, near double-digit growth for over two decades after its reforms; India's growth accelerated after 1991 but stayed below China's; Pakistan's growth slowed sharply after the 1980s due to political instability, over-dependence on remittances and foreign aid, and a volatile agricultural sector.

Sectoral structure

BasisChinaIndiaPakistan
Share of workforce in agricultureLowest of the threeHighestHigh
Leading contributor to GDP growthManufacturing and services (industry-led path: agriculture → industry → services)Services (shifted directly from agriculture to services)Services

Only about one-tenth of China's land is cultivable because of its topography and climate, yet its agriculture is productive.

Human development

  • China is ahead of India and Pakistan on income per capita, life expectancy, literacy, access to sanitation, lower infant and maternal mortality and a smaller share of people below the poverty line, and so has a higher Human Development Index rank.
  • Pakistan is ahead of India in reducing the share of people below the poverty line, but behind in education and maternal mortality.
  • Liberty indicators (democratic participation, constitutional protection of rights, independence of the judiciary) also matter; on these India performs better than China and Pakistan.

notes.heading: Appraisal: lessons from the three experiences
notes.html:
CountryWhy reforms beganOutcome
ChinaSlow growth and lack of modernisation under the Maoist system; reforms were self-initiated in 1978, without pressure from the World Bank or IMFUsed the market without losing political commitment; earlier investment in health, education and land reform gave reforms a strong base; rapid growth and poverty reduction
IndiaBalance of payments crisis of 1991; reforms under conditions of international agenciesHigher growth led by services, but agriculture still employs the largest share and poverty persists
PakistanReforms from 1988Growth slowed; poverty re-emerged because of political instability, heavy reliance on remittances and aid, and dependence on public sector enterprises

Why China did better: pre-reform creation of infrastructure in education and health, land reforms, decentralised planning and small enterprises; agricultural reform that handed plots to households brought prosperity to a vast number of poor people and created conditions for the growth of rural industries.

mcqs.q: The Great Leap Forward campaign in China was launched in
mcqs.explanation: It began in 1958 with the aim of massive industrialisation.

mcqs.q: Economic reforms were introduced in China in
mcqs.explanation: China began its reforms in 1978; Pakistan in 1988 and India in 1991.

mcqs.q: Under the commune system in China,
options: land was owned by private farmers
land was leased to foreign firms
farming was fully mechanised by the State
mcqs.explanation: Communes meant collective farming by rural people.

mcqs.q: Which country has the highest degree of urbanisation among the three?
mcqs.explanation: China is the most urbanised; India is the least of the three.

mcqs.q: In which sector does the largest share of India's workforce still work?
mcqs.explanation: Agriculture remains the biggest employer even though services contribute most to GDP.

mcqs.q: Which of the following helped Pakistan's growth in the 1980s?
mcqs.explanation: Remittances from Pakistani workers abroad and western financial support stimulated growth.

mcqs.q: The low population growth of China is mainly due to
mcqs.explanation: The one-child norm introduced in the late 1970s sharply reduced fertility.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): China's reforms were not the result of pressure from international agencies.
Reason (R): China's leadership was dissatisfied with slow growth and lack of modernisation under the earlier system.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Unlike India and Pakistan, China started reforms on its own for the reason stated in R.

questions.q: What is meant by the dual pricing system in China?
questions.answerHtml: Farmers and industrial units had to buy and sell fixed quantities of inputs and outputs at prices fixed by the government, and the rest at market prices.

questions.q: Explain the Great Leap Forward campaign of China.
questions.answerHtml:
• Launched in 1958 to industrialise the country on a massive scale.
  • People were encouraged to set up industries in their backyards.
  • In rural areas communes were started, under which people cultivated land collectively.

The campaign faced problems: a severe drought led to many deaths, and the withdrawal of Soviet professionals hurt industrial projects.

questions.q: Why did China introduce structural reforms in 1978? State the main reforms in agriculture.
questions.answerHtml:
Reason: the leadership was unhappy with slow economic growth and lack of modernisation under the Maoist system of decentralisation and self-sufficiency. The reforms were self-initiated.

Agricultural reforms: commune lands were divided into small plots and allotted to individual households for use (not ownership); households could keep all income from the land after paying the stipulated taxes.

questions.q: Compare India, China and Pakistan on any four demographic indicators.
questions.answerHtml:
• Population size: India and China have very large populations; Pakistan's is about one-tenth of either.
  • Growth rate: highest in Pakistan, lowest in China because of the one-child norm.
  • Fertility rate: very high in Pakistan, low in China.
  • Urbanisation: highest in China, lowest in India.

(Sex ratio is low and biased against females in all three because of son preference.)

questions.q: 'China has moved ahead of India and Pakistan in economic and human development.' Justify the statement with reasons for China's better performance.
questions.answerHtml:
Evidence: after 1978 China sustained near double-digit growth for over two decades, became a manufacturing-led economy, and ranks above India and Pakistan on income per capita, life expectancy, literacy, sanitation and poverty reduction.

Reasons:

  1. Strong pre-reform base: investment in education and health, land reforms and decentralised planning created infrastructure before reforms began.
  2. Agricultural reform: giving plots to households raised output and rural incomes for a vast number of poor people.
  3. Rural industries: township and village enterprises absorbed labour and supported further reform.
  4. Gradual, phased reforms: each measure was tried on a small scale and then extended.
  5. SEZs and openness to foreign investment expanded manufacturing and exports.
  6. Self-initiated reforms with strong political commitment, not imposed from outside.

However, India does better than China on liberty indicators such as democratic participation.
